q-66616.name: Question 1
q-66616.problem: Given that the function $f(x)$ has an inverse ${f}^{-1}(x)$, and the point $(5,1)$ lies on the graph $y=f(x),$ which point must lie on the graph of $y={f}^{-1}(x)?$
q-66616.worked_solution:
The function $y={f}^{-1}(x)$ is a reflection of $y=f(x)$ in the line $y=x.$ Therefore, each point $(a,b)$ on $y=f(x)$ has a corresponding point $(b,a)$ on $y={f}^{-1}(x)$ (the $x$ and $y$ coordinates swap).

Since the point $(5,1)$ lies on $y=f(x),$ the point $(1,5)$ lies on $y={f}^{-1}(x).$

q-66616.html:
Question 1
?

Given that the function f(x) has an inverse f−1(x), and the point (5,1) lies on the graph y=f(x), which point must lie on the graph of y=f−1(x)?

a
(−1,5)
b
(−1,−5)
c
(1,−5)
d
(1,5)
e
(−5,−1)
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The function y=f−1(x) is a reflection of y=f(x) in the line y=x. Therefore, each point (a,b) on y=f(x) has a corresponding point (b,a) on y=f−1(x) (the x and y coordinates swap).

Since the point (5,1) lies on y=f(x), the point (1,5) lies on y=f−1(x).

q-35205.html:
Question 2
?

Given that the function f(x) has an inverse f−1(x), and the point (−1,−3) lies on the graph y=f(x), which point must lie on the graph of y=f−1(x)?

a
(−3,1)
b
(3,1)
c
(−3,−1)
d
(1,3)
e
(3,−1)
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The function y=f−1(x) is a reflection of y=f(x) in the line y=x. Therefore, each point (a,b) on y=f(x) has a corresponding point (b,a) on y=f−1(x) (the x and y coordinates swap).

Since the point (−1,−3) lies on y=f(x), the point (−3,−1) lies on y=f−1(x).

q-35203.name: Question 3
q-35203.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14210035/assets/d8788f03a4cb07d8f447346699ed5a9e8231cc4e496e135b6df1515e56792d61.png)

The graph of ${f}^{-1}(x)$ is given above. Which of the following could be the graph of $f(x)?$
q-35203.worked_solution:
The function $y={f}^{-1}(x)$ is a reflection of $y=f(x)$ in the line $y=x.$ Of the given options, the only graph satisfying this condition is the one shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14210035/assets/ddf15053fee30ed69e2caed1a049b34c6f39c729fec0f1a053b00e33686c1e5f.png)

Notice that the points on $y=f(x)$ have corresponding points on $y={f}^{-1}(x)$ with the coordinates swapped.

$$
\begin{aligned}(0,6) & ⟶(6,0) \\ (1,4) & ⟶(4,1) \\ (2,-2) & ⟶(-2,2)\end{aligned}
$$
